---
title: "Tidy data"
---

## Packages

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
```

## What is tidy data?

![](https://github.com/allisonhorst/stats-illustrations/raw/main/rstats-artwork/tidydata_1.jpg){fig-alt="Illustration of tidy data: each variable is a column, each observation is a row, each value is a cell." width="70%"}

1. Each **variable** is a column; each column is a variable
2. Each **observation** is a row; each row is an observation
3. Each **value** is a cell; each cell is a single value

::: {.aside}
Rules from [*R for Data Science* (2e), chapter 5](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-tidy.html).
Illustration by Julia Lowndes and Allison Horst,
from the [Openscapes blog](https://www.openscapes.org/blog/2020/10/12/tidy-data/)
(CC BY 4.0).
:::

## The original definition (2014)

The original *Tidy Data* paper from 2014 defines it a little differently:

1. Each variable forms a column
2. Each observation forms a row
3. Each **type of observational unit** forms a table

The third rule is really about databases,
where data is split into separate tables and joined back together.
The newer definition replaces it with "each value is a cell".
We'll come back to observational units in Lecture 2,
in the [Observational units](/lecture-02/03-observational-units.qmd) section.

## Tidy or not? (1 of 4)

| country     | year | rate              |
|-------------|------|-------------------|
| Afghanistan | 1999 | 745/19987071      |
| Afghanistan | 2000 | 2666/20595360     |
| Brazil      | 1999 | 37737/172006362   |
| Brazil      | 2000 | 80488/174504898   |

::: {.fragment}
Not tidy.
The `rate` column has two values in each cell,
the number of cases and the population.
:::

## Tidy or not? (2 of 4)

| country     | 1999   | 2000   |
|-------------|--------|--------|
| Afghanistan | 745    | 2666   |
| Brazil      | 37737  | 80488  |
| China       | 212258 | 213766 |

::: {.fragment}
Not tidy.
The years are column headers,
but they're really values of a `year` variable.
:::

## Tidy or not? (3 of 4)

| country     | year | type       | count      |
|-------------|------|------------|------------|
| Afghanistan | 1999 | cases      | 745        |
| Afghanistan | 1999 | population | 19987071   |
| Afghanistan | 2000 | cases      | 2666       |
| Afghanistan | 2000 | population | 20595360   |

::: {.fragment}
Not tidy.
The `count` column mixes two different variables,
cases and population.
:::

## Tidy or not? (4 of 4)

| country     | year | cases  | population |
|-------------|------|--------|------------|
| Afghanistan | 1999 | 745    | 19987071   |
| Afghanistan | 2000 | 2666   | 20595360   |
| Brazil      | 1999 | 37737  | 172006362  |
| Brazil      | 2000 | 80488  | 174504898  |

::: {.fragment}
Tidy!
Each row is an observation,
each column is a variable,
and each cell has a single value.
:::

## Why bother?

![](https://github.com/allisonhorst/stats-illustrations/raw/main/rstats-artwork/tidydata_2.jpg){fig-alt="Illustration: tidy datasets are all alike, but every messy dataset is messy in its own way." width="70%"}

Once our data is tidy,
we can use the same tools every time we summarize, plot, or model it.

::: {.aside}
Illustration by Julia Lowndes and Allison Horst (CC BY 4.0).
:::

## Five ways data gets messy

The *Tidy Data* paper lists five common ways data gets messy:

1. Column headers are values, not variable names
2. Multiple variables are stored in one column
3. Variables are stored in both rows and columns
4. Multiple types of observational units are stored in the same table
5. A single observational unit is stored in multiple tables

We'll go through the first three using the datasets from the paper.
Problems 4 and 5 are about observational units,
which we'll cover in Lecture 2's
[Observational units](/lecture-02/03-observational-units.qmd) section.

## Problem 1: column headers are values

This is a Pew survey that counts people by religion and income.
The income brackets are column headers,
but they're really values of an `income` variable.

```{r}
pew <- read_csv("data/pew.csv")
pew
```

## `pivot_longer()`: wide to long

```{r}
pew_tidy <- pew |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -religion,
    names_to = "income",
    values_to = "frequency"
  )
pew_tidy
```

## Now we can summarize it

```{r}
pew_tidy |>
  group_by(religion) |>
  summarize(count = sum(frequency))
```

## Problem 1 again: the Billboard chart

Each row is a song,
and `wk1` to `wk76` hold its rank for each week it was on the chart.
The week number is a value hiding in the column headers.

```{r}
billboard <- read_csv("data/billboard.csv")
billboard
```

## Tidy the weeks

```{r}
billboard_tidy <- billboard |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "wk",
    names_transform = list(week = as.integer),
    values_to = "rank",
    values_drop_na = TRUE # drop weeks the song was not on the chart
  ) |>
  # the date at a rank = the date it entered + (week - 1) weeks
  mutate(date = date.entered + (week - 1) * 7) |>
  arrange(artist, track, week) |>
  select(year, artist, track, time, week, rank, date)
billboard_tidy
```

## Problem 2: multiple variables in one column

These are the WHO tuberculosis counts from the paper
(`who2` comes with tidyr).
A column name like `sp_m_014` has three variables in it,
the diagnosis method (`sp`), gender (`m`), and age group (`014`).

```{r}
who2
```

## Split the header into three variables

```{r}
who2 |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = !(country:year),
    names_to = c("diagnosis", "gender", "age"),
    names_sep = "_",
    values_to = "count",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  )
```

## Problem 3: variables in rows and columns

These are daily temperatures from a weather station in Mexico.
The days of the month are spread across `d1` to `d31`,
and the maximum and minimum temperatures (`tmax`, `tmin`)
are stuck in the rows of the `element` column.

```{r}
weather <- read_csv("data/weather.csv")
weather
```

## Pivot longer, then wider

```{r}
weather_tidy <- weather |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("d"),
    names_to = "day",
    names_prefix = "d",
    names_transform = list(day = as.integer),
    values_to = "temp",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  ) |>
  mutate(date = make_date(year, month, day)) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = element, # tmax and tmin become their own columns
    values_from = temp
  ) |>
  select(id, date, tmax, tmin) |>
  arrange(id, date)
weather_tidy
```

## The tidyr toolkit

| Function | Use it when |
|---|---|
| `pivot_longer()` | values are spread across column headers (wide to long) |
| `pivot_wider()` | variables are stuck in rows (long to wide) |
| `separate_wider_delim()`, or `names_sep` in `pivot_longer()` | one column or header holds several variables |
